设 $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ 与 $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ 是测度空间。称 $A\times B$（$A\in\mathcal A$、$B\in\mathcal B$）为**可测矩形**，全体记作 $\mathcal R$。乘积 $\sigma$ 代数定义为
$$\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B=\sigma(\mathcal R),$$
即包含全部可测矩形的**最小** $\sigma$ 代数。$\mathcal R$ 是 $\pi$ 系：$(A\times B)\cap(A'\times B')=(A\cap A')\times(B\cap B')$，这一性质在唯一性证明中会用到。两个投影 $\pi_X(x,y)=x$、$\pi_Y(x,y)=y$ 都关于 $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ 可测，因为 $\pi_X^{-1}(A)=A\times Y$、$\pi_Y^{-1}(B)=X\times B$；反过来，$\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ 正是使两个投影都可测的最小 $\sigma$ 代数。注意乘积 $\sigma$ 代数通常比「有限个矩形的并」大得多：$\mathbb R^2$ 的对角线 $\Delta=\{(x,x)\}$ 是闭集，属于 $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$，却不是矩形。

令 $\mathcal A_0$ 为全部「有限个两两不交的可测矩形之并」组成的集类。由矩形交仍是矩形、$(A	imes B)^c=(A^c	imes Y)\cup(A	imes B^c)$，$\mathcal A_0$ 是一个代数。在 $\mathcal A_0$ 上定义
$$\pi_0\Bigl( igsqcup_{i=1}^n A_i	imes B_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mu(A_i)
u(B_i),$$
并约定 $0\cdot\infty=0$。良定义性：若同一集合有两种有限不交矩形表示，取所有 $A_i$ 与 $B_j$ 生成的公共加细；对每个固定的 $x$ 取竖直截面，两种表示给出同一个 $E_x$ 的有限不交分解，故 $\sum_i\mathbf 1_{A_i}(x)
u(B_i)$ 相同；对 $x$ 积分即得两种和相等（也可直接由 $\mu,
u$ 的有限可加性验证）。有限可加性由定义直接得到。更重要的是，对 $E\in\mathcal A_0$ 有
$$\pi_0(E)=\int_X
u(E_x)\,d\mu(x),$$
因为矩形情形是 $
u((A	imes B)_x)=\mathbf 1_A(x)
u(B)$，有限不交并则逐项相加。于是若 $E= igsqcup_{k\ge1}E_k$ 且 $E,E_k\in\mathcal A_0$，对每个 $x$ 用 $
u$ 的可数可加性得 $
u(E_x)=\sum_k
u((E_k)_x)$，再由单调收敛定理
$$\pi_0(E)=\int_X\sum_{k\ge1}
u((E_k)_x)\,d\mu(x)=\sum_{k\ge1}\pi_0(E_k).$$
所以 $\pi_0$ 是代数 $\mathcal A_0$ 上的**预测度**（premeasure），允许取 $+\infty$。

由 Carathéodory 扩张定理，$\mathcal A_0$ 上的预测度 $\pi_0$ 可以延拓为 $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)=\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ 上的测度：先作外测度
$$ egin{aligned}
\pi^*(E)=\inf\Bigl\{&\sum_{k\ge1}\pi_0(E_k):\
&E\subseteq igcup_{k\ge1}E_k,\ E_k\in\mathcal A_0\Bigr\}.
\end{aligned}$$
然后再限制在 Carathéodory 可测集上。$\mathcal A_0$ 中每个集合都满足 Carathéodory 条件，故 $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ 中每个集合都可测，限制就是一个测度。记作 $\mu	imes
u$，称为**乘积测度**。这一步只保证**存在**，不保证唯一；这个延拓可能不是唯一的。唯一性的标准充分条件是 $\mu,
u$ 都 $\sigma$ 有限（第 5 步）；放弃它，唯一性可能失效。另外，若 $\mu,
u$ 都 $\sigma$ 有限，取 $X= igcup_m X_m$、$Y= igcup_n Y_n$ 且 $\mu(X_m),
u(Y_n)<\infty$，则 $X	imes Y= igcup_{m,n}X_m	imes Y_n$ 且 $(\mu	imes
u)(X_m	imes Y_n)<\infty$，故 $\mu	imes
u$ 也 $\sigma$ 有限。

**截面可测性**。对 $E\subseteq X	imes Y$ 与 $x\in X$、$y\in Y$，记
$$E_x=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in E\},\qquad E^y=\{x\in X:(x,y)\in E\}.$$
若 $E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$，则对**每个** $x$ 有 $E_x\in\mathcal B$，对每个 $y$ 有 $E^y\in\mathcal A$。证明：令
$$\mathcal C=\{E\subseteq X	imes Y:\ E_x\in\mathcal B,\ E^y\in\mathcal A\ 	ext{对一切 }x,y\}.$$
$\mathcal C$ 包含所有可测矩形；对补集封闭，因为 $(E^c)_x=(E_x)^c$、$(E^c)^y=(E^y)^c$；对可数并封闭，因为 $( igcup_n E_n)_x= igcup_n(E_n)_x$，$y$-截面同理。故 $\mathcal C$ 是 $\sigma$ 代数，包含 $\mathcal R$，从而包含 $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$。这说明截面可测性对每个点成立，不需要「几乎处处」。进一步，在 $\mu,
u$ 都 $\sigma$ 有限时，$x\mapsto
u(E_x)$ 是 $\mathcal A$-可测的（$y\mapsto\mu(E^y)$ 同理）：设 $Y= igcup_n Y_n$、$
u(Y_n)<\infty$，对固定的 $n$，集类
$$\mathcal D_n=\{E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B:\ x\mapsto
u(E_x\cap Y_n)\ 	ext{可测}\}$$
包含矩形；它对补集封闭用到了 $
u(Y_n)<\infty$（$
u((E^c)_x\cap Y_n)=
u(Y_n)-
u(E_x\cap Y_n)$），对不交并封闭用 $
u$ 的可数可加性，故是 $\lambda$ 系；由 $\pi$–$\lambda$ 定理，$\mathcal D_n$ 包含全部 $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$。再令 $n	o\infty$，$
u(E_x)=\lim_n
u(E_x\cap Y_n)$ 可测。

**$\sigma$ 有限时乘积测度唯一**。设 $\rho_1,\rho_2$ 是 $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ 上的两个测度，且对一切可测矩形有 $\rho_1(A\times B)=\rho_2(A\times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B)$。取 $X_m\uparrow X$、$Y_n\uparrow Y$ 且 $\mu(X_m),\nu(Y_n)<\infty$。固定 $m,n$，令
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathcal D_{mn}=\bigl\{E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B:\ 
&\rho_1(E\cap(X_m\times Y_n))\\
&=\rho_2(E\cap(X_m\times Y_n))\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}$$
它包含矩形，因为 $(A\times B)\cap(X_m\times Y_n)=(A\cap X_m)\times(B\cap Y_n)$；对补集封闭，因为两个测度在 $X_m\times Y_n$ 上都有限；对不交并封闭由可数可加性。故 $\mathcal D_{mn}$ 是 $\lambda$ 系，由 $\pi$–$\lambda$ 定理包含全部 $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$。再令 $m,n\to\infty$，由测度的下方连续性得 $\rho_1(E)=\rho_2(E)$。所以 $\mu\times\nu$ 由矩形上的值唯一确定。

没有 $\sigma$ 有限性时唯一性会失败。取 $X=Y=[0,1]$、$\mathcal A=\mathcal B=\mathcal B([0,1])$、$\mu$ 为勒贝格测度、$\nu$ 为计数测度（不 $\sigma$ 有限）。定义
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho_1(E)&=\int_0^1\#(E_x)\,d\mu(x),\\
\rho_2(E)&=\int_{[0,1]}\mu(E^y)\,d\nu(y)=\sum_{y\in[0,1]}\mu(E^y).
\end{aligned}$$
对可测矩形 $A\times B$，两者都等于 $\mu(A)\#B$；但对角线 $\Delta=\{(x,x)\}$ 有 $\rho_1(\Delta)=1$、$\rho_2(\Delta)=0$。故矩形上的值不能唯一确定测度。（$\rho_1$ 中的 $x\mapsto\#E_x$ 对 Borel 集 $E$ 是普遍可测的；$\rho_2$ 是诸测度 $E\mapsto\mu(E^y)$ 的和。）

在 $\sigma$ 有限条件下，截面测度可以积分还原乘积测度：对 $E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$，
$$(\mu	imes
u)(E)=\int_X
u(E_x)\,d\mu(x)=\int_Y\mu(E^y)\,d
u(y).$$
证明：由第 4 步，$x\mapsto
u(E_x)$ 可测；令 $ho(E)=\int_X
u(E_x)\,d\mu(x)$。对不交并 $E= igsqcup_k E_k$，由 $
u$ 的可数可加性与单调收敛定理，$ho(E)=\sum_kho(E_k)$，故 $ho$ 是测度。对矩形 $A	imes B$，$ho(A	imes B)=\int_A
u(B)\,d\mu=\mu(A)
u(B)$；由第 5 步的唯一性，$ho=\mu	imes
u$。另一半对称。这个公式是 Tonelli 定理的集合版本。例：$[0,1]^2$ 中的三角形 $E=\{(x,y):x+y<1\}$，$E_x=[0,1-x)$，故
$$(\mu	imes
u)(E)=\int_0^1(1-x)\,dx= rac12.$$
注意：没有 $\sigma$ 有限性时公式可能失效；第 5 步的对角线例子中 $ho_1(\Delta)=1$ 而 $ho_2(\Delta)=0$，正说明两个截面积分不必相等。
en:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be measure spaces. A set $A\times B$ with $A\in\mathcal A$ and $B\in\mathcal B$ is called a **measurable rectangle**; let $\mathcal R$ be the family of all of them. The product $\sigma$-algebra is
$$\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B=\sigma(\mathcal R),$$
the smallest $\sigma$-algebra containing every measurable rectangle. The family $\mathcal R$ is a $\pi$-system: $(A\times B)\cap(A'\times B')=(A\cap A')\times(B\cap B')$, a fact used in the uniqueness proof. The projections $\pi_X(x,y)=x$ and $\pi_Y(x,y)=y$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$, since $\pi_X^{-1}(A)=A\times Y$ and $\pi_Y^{-1}(B)=X\times B$; conversely, $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra making both projections measurable. The product $\sigma$-algebra is usually much larger than finite unions of rectangles: the diagonal $\Delta=\{(x,x)\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ is closed, hence Borel, but is not a rectangle.

Let $\mathcal A_0$ be the class of all finite unions of pairwise disjoint measurable rectangles. Since intersections of rectangles are rectangles and $(A	imes B)^c=(A^c	imes Y)\cup(A	imes B^c)$, $\mathcal A_0$ is an algebra. Define on $\mathcal A_0$
$$\pi_0\Bigl( igsqcup_{i=1}^n A_i	imes B_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mu(A_i)
u(B_i),$$
with the convention $0\cdot\infty=0$. Well-definedness: if the same set has two finite disjoint rectangle representations, pass to the common refinement generated by all the $A_i$'s and $B_j$'s; for each fixed $x$, taking the vertical section gives two finite disjoint decompositions of the same set $E_x$, so $\sum_i\mathbf 1_{A_i}(x)
u(B_i)$ is the same for both; integrating in $x$ gives equality of the two sums (one may also check this directly from finite additivity of $\mu$ and $
u$). Finite additivity is immediate from the definition. More importantly, for $E\in\mathcal A_0$,
$$\pi_0(E)=\int_X
u(E_x)\,d\mu(x),$$
since for a rectangle $
u((A	imes B)_x)=\mathbf 1_A(x)
u(B)$, and finite disjoint unions add. Hence if $E= igsqcup_{k\ge1}E_k$ with $E,E_k\in\mathcal A_0$, then for each $x$ countable additivity of $
u$ gives $
u(E_x)=\sum_k
u((E_k)_x)$, and monotone convergence yields
$$\pi_0(E)=\int_X\sum_{k\ge1}
u((E_k)_x)\,d\mu(x)=\sum_{k\ge1}\pi_0(E_k).$$
Thus $\pi_0$ is a **premeasure** on $\mathcal A_0$, allowed to take $+\infty$.

By the Carathéodory extension theorem, the premeasure $\pi_0$ on $\mathcal A_0$ extends to a measure on $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)=\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$: first form the outer measure
$$\begin{aligned}
\pi^*(E)=\inf\Bigl\{&\sum_{k\ge1}\pi_0(E_k):\\
&E\subseteq\bigcup_{k\ge1}E_k,\ E_k\in\mathcal A_0\Bigr\}.
\end{aligned}$$
Then restrict it to the Carathéodory measurable sets. Every set in $\mathcal A_0$ satisfies the Carathéodory condition, so every set in $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ is measurable and the restriction is a measure. It is denoted $\mu\times\nu$ and called the **product measure**. This step gives existence only, not uniqueness: the extension need not be unique. A standard sufficient condition for uniqueness is that both $\mu$ and $\nu$ are $\sigma$-finite (Step 5); without it, uniqueness can fail. If both are $\sigma$-finite, write $X=\bigcup_m X_m$ and $Y=\bigcup_n Y_n$ with $\mu(X_m),\nu(Y_n)<\infty$; then $X\times Y=\bigcup_{m,n}X_m\times Y_n$ and $(\mu\times\nu)(X_m\times Y_n)<\infty$, so $\mu\times\nu$ is $\sigma$-finite too.

**Measurability of sections.** For $E\subseteq X	imes Y$, $x\in X$ and $y\in Y$, set
$$E_x=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in E\},\qquad E^y=\{x\in X:(x,y)\in E\}.$$
If $E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$, then $E_x\in\mathcal B$ for **every** $x$ and $E^y\in\mathcal A$ for every $y$. Indeed, let
$$\mathcal C=\{E\subseteq X	imes Y:\ E_x\in\mathcal B,\ E^y\in\mathcal A\ 	ext{for all }x,y\}.$$
It contains every measurable rectangle; it is closed under complements because $(E^c)_x=(E_x)^c$ and $(E^c)^y=(E^y)^c$; and it is closed under countable unions because $( igcup_n E_n)_x= igcup_n(E_n)_x$, and similarly for $y$-sections. Hence $\mathcal C$ is a $\sigma$-algebra containing $\mathcal R$, so it contains $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$. Thus sections are measurable at every point, not merely almost every point. Moreover, if $\mu$ and $
u$ are $\sigma$-finite, $x\mapsto
u(E_x)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable (and $y\mapsto\mu(E^y)$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable). To see this, write $Y= igcup_n Y_n$ with $
u(Y_n)<\infty$ and, for fixed $n$, let
$$\mathcal D_n=\{E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B:\ x\mapsto
u(E_x\cap Y_n)\ 	ext{is measurable}\}.$$
It contains rectangles; it is closed under complements because $
u(Y_n)<\infty$ gives $
u((E^c)_x\cap Y_n)=
u(Y_n)-
u(E_x\cap Y_n)$; and it is closed under disjoint countable unions by countable additivity of $
u$. Hence $\mathcal D_n$ is a $\lambda$-system, and the $\pi$–$\lambda$ theorem gives $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal D_n$. Letting $n	o\infty$, $
u(E_x)=\lim_n
u(E_x\cap Y_n)$ is measurable.

**Uniqueness under $\sigma$-finiteness.** Let $\rho_1,\rho_2$ be measures on $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ with $\rho_1(A\times B)=\rho_2(A\times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B)$ for every measurable rectangle. Take $X_m\uparrow X$ and $Y_n\uparrow Y$ with $\mu(X_m),\nu(Y_n)<\infty$. For fixed $m,n$, put
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathcal D_{mn}=\bigl\{E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B:\ 
&\rho_1(E\cap(X_m\times Y_n))\\
&=\rho_2(E\cap(X_m\times Y_n))\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}$$
It contains rectangles, since $(A\times B)\cap(X_m\times Y_n)=(A\cap X_m)\times(B\cap Y_n)$; it is closed under complements because both measures are finite on $X_m\times Y_n$; and it is closed under disjoint countable unions by countable additivity. Thus $\mathcal D_{mn}$ is a $\lambda$-system, and the $\pi$–$\lambda$ theorem gives all of $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$. Letting $m,n\to\infty$ and using continuity from below gives $\rho_1(E)=\rho_2(E)$. Hence $\mu\times\nu$ is uniquely determined by its values on rectangles.

Without $\sigma$-finiteness uniqueness can fail. Take $X=Y=[0,1]$, $\mathcal A=\mathcal B=\mathcal B([0,1])$, $\mu$ Lebesgue measure and $\nu$ counting measure (not $\sigma$-finite). Define
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho_1(E)&=\int_0^1\#(E_x)\,d\mu(x),\\
\rho_2(E)&=\int_{[0,1]}\mu(E^y)\,d\nu(y)=\sum_{y\in[0,1]}\mu(E^y).
\end{aligned}$$
On a measurable rectangle $A\times B$ both equal $\mu(A)\#B$; but on the diagonal $\Delta=\{(x,x)\}$ we have $\rho_1(\Delta)=1$ and $\rho_2(\Delta)=0$. Thus the rectangle values do not determine the measure. (Here $x\mapsto\#E_x$ is universally measurable for Borel $E$, and $\rho_2$ is a sum of the measures $E\mapsto\mu(E^y)$.)

Under $\sigma$-finiteness, section measures integrate back to the product measure: for $E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$,
$$(\mu	imes
u)(E)=\int_X
u(E_x)\,d\mu(x)=\int_Y\mu(E^y)\,d
u(y).$$
Proof: by Step 4, $x\mapsto
u(E_x)$ is measurable; set $ho(E)=\int_X
u(E_x)\,d\mu(x)$. For a disjoint union $E= igsqcup_k E_k$, countable additivity of $
u$ and monotone convergence give $ho(E)=\sum_kho(E_k)$, so $ho$ is a measure. For a rectangle $A	imes B$, $ho(A	imes B)=\int_A
u(B)\,d\mu=\mu(A)
u(B)$; by uniqueness (Step 5), $ho=\mu	imes
u$. The other direction is symmetric. This formula is the set-theoretic form of Tonelli's theorem. Example: for the triangle $E=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:x+y<1\}$, $E_x=[0,1-x)$, so
$$(\mu	imes
u)(E)=\int_0^1(1-x)\,dx= rac12.$$
Without $\sigma$-finiteness the formula can fail: in the diagonal example of Step 5, $ho_1(\Delta)=1$ while $ho_2(\Delta)=0$, so the two section integrals need not agree.

设 $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$、$(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ 都是 $\sigma$ 有限测度空间，$f$ 是 $(X\times Y,\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B)$ 上的可测函数。我们比较三个积分：
$$\begin{aligned}
&\int_{X\times Y}f\,d(\mu\times\nu),\\
&\int_X\Bigl(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)\Bigr)d\mu(x),\\
&\int_Y\Bigl(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\Bigr)d\nu(y).
\end{aligned}$$
**Tonelli 定理**：若 $f\ge0$ 可测（允许 $+\infty$），则对每个 $x$，$f(x,\cdot)$ 可测；$x\mapsto\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)$ 与 $y\mapsto\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)$ 都可测；并且
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_X\!\!\int_Y f\,d\nu\,d\mu
&=\int_{X\times Y}f\,d(\mu\times\nu)\\
&=\int_Y\!\!\int_X f\,d\mu\,d\nu,
\end{aligned}$$
三者在 $[0,+\infty]$ 中相等。**不要求 $f$ 可积**，也不要求 $\mu(X),\nu(Y)<\infty$，只要求 $\sigma$ 有限。**Fubini 定理**：若 $\int_{X\times Y}|f|\,d(\mu\times\nu)<+\infty$，则对 $\mu$-a.e. $x$ 有 $\int_Y|f(x,y)|\,d\nu(y)<+\infty$，函数 $x\mapsto\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)$ 属于 $L^1(\mu)$，$y$-方向对称，并且上述三个积分相等且为有限实数。

先对示性函数证明 Tonelli。设 $E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$，$f=\mathbf 1_E$。由截面可测性，$E_x\in\mathcal B$、$E^y\in\mathcal A$ 对每个点成立；由 $\sigma$ 有限性，$x\mapsto
u(E_x)$、$y\mapsto\mu(E^y)$ 可测。乘积测度的截面积分公式给出
$$(\mu	imes
u)(E)=\int_X
u(E_x)\,d\mu(x)=\int_Y\mu(E^y)\,d
u(y).$$
而 $\int_{X	imes Y}\mathbf 1_E\,d(\mu	imes
u)=(\mu	imes
u)(E)$，且
$$\int_Y\mathbf 1_E(x,y)\,d
u(y)=
u(E_x),\qquad
\int_X\mathbf 1_E(x,y)\,d\mu(x)=\mu(E^y).$$
所以三个积分相等，允许取 $+\infty$。这是 Tonelli 的基例；这里没有用到 $E$ 的测度有限。

对非负简单函数 $s=\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\mathbf 1_{E_k}$（$E_k$ 两两不交，$0\le a_k<+\infty$），由积分的线性性和第 2 步，
$$\begin{aligned}
\int s\,d(\mu\times\nu)
&=\sum_k a_k(\mu\times\nu)(E_k)\\
&=\int_X\!\!\int_Y s\,d\nu\,d\mu=\int_Y\!\!\int_X s\,d\mu\,d\nu.
\end{aligned}$$
对一般非负可测 $f$，取非负简单函数 $s_n\uparrow f$（例如 $s_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n2^n}\frac{j-1}{2^n}\mathbf 1_{\{(j-1)/2^n\le f<j/2^n\}}+n\mathbf 1_{\{f\ge n\}}$）。对每个 $n$，上式对 $s_n$ 成立。令 $n\to\infty$：由单调收敛定理，
$$\int f\,d(\mu\times\nu)=\lim_n\int s_n\,d(\mu\times\nu).$$
固定 $x$，$s_n(x,\cdot)\uparrow f(x,\cdot)$，故 $\int_Y s_n(x,\cdot)\,d\nu\uparrow\int_Y f(x,\cdot)\,d\nu$；右边作为可测函数的极限可测。再对 $x$ 用单调收敛定理，得
$$\int_X\!\!\int_Y s_n\,d\nu\,d\mu\uparrow\int_X\!\!\int_Y f\,d\nu\,d\mu.$$
于是第一个累次积分等于二重积分；$y$-方向同理。全过程在 $[0,+\infty]$ 中进行，$+\infty$ 也可以取到，不需要控制收敛。

现在证 Fubini。设 $f\in L^1(\mu	imes
u)$。对 $|f|\ge0$ 用 Tonelli：
$$\int_X\Bigl(\int_Y|f(x,y)|\,d
u(y)\Bigr)d\mu(x)=\int_{X	imes Y}|f|\,d(\mu	imes
u)<+\infty.$$
非负函数若积分有限，则几乎处处有限；故 $\int_Y|f(x,y)|\,d
u(y)<+\infty$ 对 $\mu$-a.e. $x$ 成立，$y$-方向同理。于是 $f^+,f^-$ 的非负累次积分都有限（它们不超过 $|f|$ 的对应积分），可以对 $f^+,f^-$ 分别用 Tonelli 再相减：
$$ egin{aligned}
\int_X\!\!\int_Y f\,d
u\,d\mu
&=\int_X\!\!\int_Y f^+\,d
u\,d\mu\
&\quad-\int_X\!\!\int_Y f^-\,d
u\,d\mu\
&=\int f^+\,d(\mu	imes
u)-\int f^-\,d(\mu	imes
u)\
&=\int f\,d(\mu	imes
u).
\end{aligned}$$
并且
$$\int_X\Bigl|\int_Y f\,d
u\Bigr|d\mu\le\int_X\!\!\int_Y|f|\,d
u\,d\mu=\int|f|<+\infty,$$
所以 $x\mapsto\int_Y f(x,y)\,d
u(y)\in L^1(\mu)$。三个积分都是有限实数，$y$-方向对称。关键：可积性假设是对 $|f|$ 的整体假设，不是「某一个累次积分有限」；后者不能保证另一个次序有意义，更不能保证相等。

反例说明「只验一个累次积分有限」不够。在 $(0,1)^2$ 上取
$$f(x,y)=\frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}.$$
对固定 $x>0$，
$$\int_0^1 f(x,y)\,dy=\Bigl[\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}\Bigr]_{0}^{1}=\frac{1}{1+x^2},$$
故
$$\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 f\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\frac{\pi}{4}.$$
另一个次序：$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[-\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\bigr]=f(x,y)$，故
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 f(x,y)\,dx&=\Bigl[-\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\Bigr]_{0}^{1}=-\frac{1}{1+y^2},\\
\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 f\,dx\,dy&=-\frac{\pi}{4}.
\end{aligned}$$
两个累次积分都存在且有限，却不相等。原因不是计算错误，而是 $f\notin L^1$：当 $0<y<x/2$ 时，
$$x^2-y^2\ge\frac34x^2,\qquad (x^2+y^2)^2\le\Bigl(\frac54x^2\Bigr)^2=\frac{25}{16}x^4,$$
故 $|f|\ge\frac{12}{25x^2}$，从而
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^{x/2}|f(x,y)|\,dy
&\ge\frac{12}{25x^2}\cdot\frac{x}{2}=\frac{6}{25x},\\
\iint_{(0,1)^2}|f|
&\ge\frac{6}{25}\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x}=+\infty.
\end{aligned}$$
Fubini 的绝对可积条件失效，交换次序当然没有保证。

$\sigma$ 有限性不能去掉。取 $X=Y=[0,1]$、$\mu$ 为勒贝格测度、$\nu$ 为计数测度，$f=\mathbf 1_\Delta$，其中 $\Delta=\{(x,x)\}$。则
$$\int_X\!\!\int_Y f\,d\nu\,d\mu=\int_0^1 1\,d\mu(x)=1,$$
因为 $\Delta_x=\{x\}$ 的计数测度为 $1$；而
$$\int_Y\!\!\int_X f\,d\mu\,d\nu=\int_{[0,1]}0\,d\nu(y)=0,$$
因为 $\Delta^y=\{y\}$ 的勒贝格测度为 $0$。两个累次积分都有定义却不相等；这里 $\nu$ 不 $\sigma$ 有限，Tonelli 的结论失效（$f\ge0$），而两个累次积分不等也说明 Fubini 的绝对可积性不可能成立。另一个常用推论是层饼公式：对 $f\ge0$ 可测，
$$\int_X f\,d\mu=\int_0^{+\infty}\mu(\{f>t\})\,dt,$$
它把 $f(x)=\int_0^{f(x)}dt$ 写成 $X\times(0,+\infty)$ 上的示性函数积分，再用 Tonelli 交换次序；这里两个测度都 $\sigma$ 有限，且非负性保证 $+\infty$ 也可以比较。

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be $\sigma$-finite measure spaces, and let $f$ be measurable on $(X\times Y,\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B)$. We compare the three integrals
$$\begin{aligned}
&\int_{X\times Y}f\,d(\mu\times\nu),\\
&\int_X\Bigl(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)\Bigr)d\mu(x),\\
&\int_Y\Bigl(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\Bigr)d\nu(y).
\end{aligned}$$
**Tonelli's theorem**: if $f\ge0$ is measurable (possibly $+\infty$), then $f(x,\cdot)$ is measurable for every $x$; the functions $x\mapsto\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)$ and $y\mapsto\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)$ are measurable; and
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_X\!\!\int_Y f\,d\nu\,d\mu
&=\int_{X\times Y}f\,d(\mu\times\nu)\\
&=\int_Y\!\!\int_X f\,d\mu\,d\nu,
\end{aligned}$$
all three equal in $[0,+\infty]$. No integrability of $f$ is required, and $\mu(X),\nu(Y)$ need not be finite; only $\sigma$-finiteness is assumed. **Fubini's theorem**: if $\int_{X\times Y}|f|\,d(\mu\times\nu)<+\infty$, then $\int_Y|f(x,y)|\,d\nu(y)<+\infty$ for $\mu$-a.e. $x$, the function $x\mapsto\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$, the symmetric statement holds in $y$, and the three integrals above are equal finite real numbers.

First prove Tonelli for indicators. Let $E\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B$ and $f=\mathbf 1_E$. By section measurability, $E_x\in\mathcal B$ and $E^y\in\mathcal A$ for every point; by $\sigma$-finiteness, $x\mapsto
u(E_x)$ and $y\mapsto\mu(E^y)$ are measurable. The section-integration formula for the product measure gives
$$(\mu	imes
u)(E)=\int_X
u(E_x)\,d\mu(x)=\int_Y\mu(E^y)\,d
u(y).$$
Since $\int_{X	imes Y}\mathbf 1_E\,d(\mu	imes
u)=(\mu	imes
u)(E)$ and
$$\int_Y\mathbf 1_E(x,y)\,d
u(y)=
u(E_x),\qquad
\int_X\mathbf 1_E(x,y)\,d\mu(x)=\mu(E^y),$$
the three integrals coincide, possibly at $+\infty$. This is the base case of Tonelli; no finiteness of $E$ was used.

For a nonnegative simple function $s=\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\mathbf 1_{E_k}$ with pairwise disjoint $E_k$ and $0\le a_k<+\infty$, linearity and Step 2 give
$$\begin{aligned}
\int s\,d(\mu\times\nu)
&=\sum_k a_k(\mu\times\nu)(E_k)\\
&=\int_X\!\!\int_Y s\,d\nu\,d\mu=\int_Y\!\!\int_X s\,d\mu\,d\nu.
\end{aligned}$$
For a general nonnegative measurable $f$, choose nonnegative simple functions $s_n\uparrow f$ (for instance $s_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n2^n}\frac{j-1}{2^n}\mathbf 1_{\{(j-1)/2^n\le f<j/2^n\}}+n\mathbf 1_{\{f\ge n\}}$). The identity holds for each $s_n$. Letting $n\to\infty$, monotone convergence gives
$$\int f\,d(\mu\times\nu)=\lim_n\int s_n\,d(\mu\times\nu).$$
For fixed $x$, $s_n(x,\cdot)\uparrow f(x,\cdot)$, so $\int_Y s_n(x,\cdot)\,d\nu\uparrow\int_Y f(x,\cdot)\,d\nu$; the right side is measurable as a limit of measurable functions. Applying monotone convergence in $x$,
$$\int_X\!\!\int_Y s_n\,d\nu\,d\mu\uparrow\int_X\!\!\int_Y f\,d\nu\,d\mu.$$
Hence the first iterated integral equals the double integral; the $y$-direction is the same. Everything takes place in $[0,+\infty]$, so $+\infty$ is allowed and no dominated convergence is needed.

Now prove Fubini. Let $f\in L^1(\mu	imes
u)$. Apply Tonelli to $|f|\ge0$:
$$\int_X\Bigl(\int_Y|f(x,y)|\,d
u(y)\Bigr)d\mu(x)=\int_{X	imes Y}|f|\,d(\mu	imes
u)<+\infty.$$
A nonnegative function with finite integral is finite almost everywhere; hence $\int_Y|f(x,y)|\,d
u(y)<+\infty$ for $\mu$-a.e. $x$, and symmetrically in $y$. Thus the nonnegative iterated integrals of $f^+$ and $f^-$ are finite (they are bounded by the corresponding integrals of $|f|$), and Tonelli applied to $f^+$ and $f^-$ followed by subtraction gives
$$ egin{aligned}
\int_X\!\!\int_Y f\,d
u\,d\mu
&=\int_X\!\!\int_Y f^+\,d
u\,d\mu\
&\quad-\int_X\!\!\int_Y f^-\,d
u\,d\mu\
&=\int f^+\,d(\mu	imes
u)-\int f^-\,d(\mu	imes
u)\
&=\int f\,d(\mu	imes
u).
\end{aligned}$$
Moreover,
$$\int_X\Bigl|\int_Y f\,d
u\Bigr|d\mu\le\int_X\!\!\int_Y|f|\,d
u\,d\mu=\int|f|<+\infty,$$
so $x\mapsto\int_Y f(x,y)\,d
u(y)\in L^1(\mu)$. All three integrals are finite real numbers, and the $y$-direction is symmetric. The key point: the hypothesis is absolute integrability of $f$ as a whole, not finiteness of one iterated integral; the latter neither guarantees that the other order is defined nor that the two orders agree.

A counterexample shows that checking one iterated integral is not enough. On $(0,1)^2$ take
$$f(x,y)=\frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}.$$
For fixed $x>0$,
$$\int_0^1 f(x,y)\,dy=\Bigl[\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}\Bigr]_{0}^{1}=\frac{1}{1+x^2},$$
so
$$\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 f\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\frac{\pi}{4}.$$
In the other order, $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\bigl[-\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\bigr]=f(x,y)$, hence
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 f(x,y)\,dx&=\Bigl[-\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\Bigr]_{0}^{1}=-\frac{1}{1+y^2},\\
\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 f\,dx\,dy&=-\frac{\pi}{4}.
\end{aligned}$$
Both iterated integrals exist and are finite, yet they differ. The reason is that $f\notin L^1$: for $0<y<x/2$,
$$x^2-y^2\ge\frac34x^2,\qquad (x^2+y^2)^2\le\Bigl(\frac54x^2\Bigr)^2=\frac{25}{16}x^4,$$
so $|f|\ge\frac{12}{25x^2}$, and therefore
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_0^{x/2}|f(x,y)|\,dy
&\ge\frac{12}{25x^2}\cdot\frac{x}{2}=\frac{6}{25x},\\
\iint_{(0,1)^2}|f|
&\ge\frac{6}{25}\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x}=+\infty.
\end{aligned}$$
Fubini's absolute integrability hypothesis fails, so there is no contradiction.

$\sigma$-finiteness cannot be dropped. Take $X=Y=[0,1]$, $\mu$ Lebesgue measure, $\nu$ counting measure, and $f=\mathbf 1_\Delta$ with $\Delta=\{(x,x)\}$. Then
$$\int_X\!\!\int_Y f\,d\nu\,d\mu=\int_0^1 1\,d\mu(x)=1,$$
because $\Delta_x=\{x\}$ has counting measure $1$, while
$$\int_Y\!\!\int_X f\,d\mu\,d\nu=\int_{[0,1]}0\,d\nu(y)=0,$$
because $\Delta^y=\{y\}$ has Lebesgue measure $0$. Both iterated integrals are defined but unequal; here $\nu$ is not $\sigma$-finite, so Tonelli's conclusion fails for the nonnegative $f$, and the inequality of the two iterated integrals shows that Fubini's absolute integrability cannot hold either. Another standard consequence is the layer-cake formula: for nonnegative measurable $f$,
$$\int_X f\,d\mu=\int_0^{+\infty}\mu(\{f>t\})\,dt,$$
obtained by writing $f(x)=\int_0^{f(x)}dt$ as an integral of an indicator on $X\times(0,+\infty)$ and applying Tonelli; both measures are $\sigma$-finite, and nonnegativity allows $+\infty$ on both sides.

设 $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$。对分割 $P:a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$，记变差和
$$S_P(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|,\qquad
V_a^b(f)=\sup_P S_P(f).$$
若 $V_a^b(f)<+\infty$，称 $f$ 在 $[a,b]$ 上**有界变差**，记 $f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]$。立刻得到：取只有两个点的分割，$V_a^b(f)\ge|f(b)-f(a)|$；$V_a^b(f)=0$ 当且仅当 $f$ 为常数；单调时 $V_a^b(f)=|f(b)-f(a)|$（单调增时变差和 telescoping 为 $f(b)-f(a)$，且每项非负）。并且 $f\in\mathrm{BV}$ 必有界：
$$|f(x)|\le|f(a)|+|f(x)-f(a)|\le|f(a)|+V_a^x(f)\le|f(a)|+V_a^b(f).$$
还要记住区间可加性：对 $a<c<b$，
$$V_a^b(f)=V_a^c(f)+V_c^b(f).$$
证明：任何 $[a,b]$ 的分割加入 $c$ 后变差和不减，故上确界可在含 $c$ 的分割上取；含 $c$ 的分割的变差和正好分成 $[a,c]$ 与 $[c,b]$ 两段之和，分别取上确界即得。

**Jordan 分解**。若 $f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]$，令
$$F(x)=V_a^x(f),\qquad G(x)=F(x)-f(x).$$
由区间可加性，$x<y$ 时 $F(y)-F(x)=V_x^y(f)\ge0$，故 $F$ 单调增；又
$$G(y)-G(x)=V_x^y(f)-\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)\ge|f(y)-f(x)|-\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)\ge0,$$
故 $G$ 也单调增。于是 $f=F-G$ 是两个单调增函数之差。反过来，若 $f=f_1-f_2$ 且 $f_1,f_2$ 单调增，则对任意分割，
$$\begin{aligned}
\sum_i|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|
&\le\sum_i|f_1(x_i)-f_1(x_{i-1})|\\
&\quad+\sum_i|f_2(x_i)-f_2(x_{i-1})|\\
&=(f_1(b)-f_1(a))+(f_2(b)-f_2(a))<+\infty,
\end{aligned}$$
故 $f\in\mathrm{BV}$。所以
$$f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]\iff f=f_1-f_2,\quad f_1,f_2\ \text{单调增}.$$
分解不唯一（两边同加一个单调增函数仍成立）。若取对称分解
$$f_1=\frac{V_a^x(f)+f(x)}2,\qquad f_2=\frac{V_a^x(f)-f(x)}2,$$
则 $f_1,f_2$ 单调增，且总增量恰为 $f_1(b)-f_1(a)+f_2(b)-f_2(a)=V_a^b(f)$。

**间断结构**。设 $f\in\mathrm{BV}$，由 Jordan 分解 $f=f_1-f_2$，$f_1,f_2$ 单调增。单调函数在每点有单侧极限：$g(x-)=\sup_{t<x}g(t)$、$g(x+)=\inf_{t>x}g(t)$（在端点只取相应一侧），故 $f$ 在每点的左右极限都存在。若 $g$ 在 $x$ 间断，则 $g(x-)<g(x+)$，称跳跃；对 $x<y$ 有 $g(x+)\le g(y-)$，所以跳跃区间 $(g(x-),g(x+))$ 两两不交。每个非空开区间含一个有理数，故单调函数的间断点至多可数。于是 $$D(f)\subseteq D(f_1)\cup D(f_2)$$ 也至多可数。间断点可以是跳跃（左右极限不等），也可以是可去间断（左右极限相等但函数值不同）：例如 $f(1/2)=1$、其余点为 $0$ 的函数属于 BV，但在 $1/2$ 处是可去间断。取右连续版本 $f^+(x)=f(x+)$（端点适当定义），它只改至多可数多个点；此后所有间断都是跳跃型，不会出现 $\sin\frac1x$ 那样的振荡型间断。作为对比，$$g(x)=\sin\frac1x\ (x>0),\qquad g(0)=0$$ 在 $[0,1]$ 上有界且除 $0$ 外连续，但取 $x_k=\frac{1}{\pi/2+k\pi}$ 时 $g(x_k)=(-1)^k$，变差和至少 $2(N-1)$，故 $V_0^1(g)=+\infty$：有界、甚至连续，都不足以保证有界变差。

**几乎处处可导（Lebesgue）**。定理：$[a,b]$ 上的单调函数几乎处处可导，且若 $g$ 单调增，则 $g'\ge0$ a.e. 且
$$\int_a^b g'(t)\,dt\le g(b)-g(a).$$
证明要点：对单调增 $g$，考虑四个 Dini 导数，例如
$$D^+g(x)=\limsup_{h\to0+}\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}h,\qquad
D_-g(x)=\liminf_{h\to0-}\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}h,$$
以及另外两个；用 Vitali 覆盖引理可证任意两个 Dini 导数不相等的点集为 null，故四者在 a.e. 处相等，记为 $g'$。积分不等式可由 Fatou 引理得到：把 $g$ 在 $[a,b]$ 外作常数延拓，则
$$\int_a^b\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}h\,dx=\frac1h\Bigl(\int_b^{b+h}g-\int_a^{a+h}g\Bigr)=g(b)-g(a),$$
令 $h\to0+$ 并用 Fatou 即得。对 $f\in\mathrm{BV}$，由 Jordan 分解 $f=f_1-f_2$，两个单调函数都 a.e. 可导，故 $f'$ 存在 a.e.。注意：结论是几乎处处，不是处处；跳跃点（至多可数）可以不可导。

**导数的可积性与变差比较**。由第 4 步，$f\in\mathrm{BV}$ 时 $f'$ 存在 a.e.；又 $f'$ 是差商 $n(f(x+1/n)-f(x))$ 的 a.e. 极限（把 $f$ 在 $[a,b]$ 外作常数延拓），故可测。取对称 Jordan 分解
$$f_1=\frac{V_a^x(f)+f(x)}2,\qquad f_2=\frac{V_a^x(f)-f(x)}2,$$
则 $f_1,f_2$ 单调增，$f=f_1-f_2$，且
$$f_1(b)-f_1(a)+f_2(b)-f_2(a)=V_a^b(f).$$
由第 4 步，$f_1',f_2'\ge0$ a.e.，且 $\int_a^b f_i'\le f_i(b)-f_i(a)$。于是 $f'=f_1'-f_2'$ a.e.，从而 $|f'|\le f_1'+f_2'$ a.e.，故
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_a^b|f'(t)|\,dt
&\le\int_a^b f_1'(t)\,dt+\int_a^b f_2'(t)\,dt\\
&\le[f_1(b)-f_1(a)]+[f_2(b)-f_2(a)]=V_a^b(f).
\end{aligned}$$
特别地 $f'\in L^1(a,b)$。这个不等式可能严格：$g=\mathbf 1_{(1/2,1]}$ 在 $[0,1]$ 上满足 $V_0^1(g)=1$，但 $g'=0$ a.e.，故 $\int_0^1|g'|=0<1$。跳跃被全变差记录，却不进入导数。

**等号刻画绝对连续**。对 $f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]$，有 $$V_a^b(f)\ge\int_a^b|f'(t)|\,dt,$$ 等号成立当且仅当 $f$ 绝对连续。证明：令 $V(x)=V_a^x(f)$，并定义 $$g(x)=\frac{V(x)+f(x)}2,\qquad h(x)=\frac{V(x)-f(x)}2.$$ 对 $x<y$，由区间可加性 $V(y)-V(x)=V_x^y(f)\ge|f(y)-f(x)|$，故 $g,h$ 都单调不减；且 $f=g-h$、$g+h=V$。于是 $$g(b)-g(a)+h(b)-h(a)=V_a^b(f).$$ 单调函数 a.e. 可导，故 $f'=g'-h'$ a.e.，且 $g',h'\ge0$。由单调函数的微积分不等式 $\int_a^b g'\le g(b)-g(a)$、$\int_a^b h'\le h(b)-h(a)$，得 $$\int_a^b|f'|\le\int_a^b(g'+h')\le V_a^b(f).$$ 若 $f$ 绝对连续，则对任意分割 $\sum_i|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|\le\sum_i\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i}|f'|=\int_a^b|f'|$，故 $V_a^b(f)\le\int_a^b|f'|$，与已证反向不等式合并得等号成立。反之若等号成立，令 $H(x)=V(x)-\int_a^x|f'|$；对任意 $x<y$，在 $[x,y]$ 上用上面的不等式得 $H(y)\ge H(x)$，且 $H\ge0$、$H(b)=0$，故 $H\equiv0$。于是 $V(x)=\int_a^x|f'|$ 绝对连续；由 $g+h=V$ 且 $g,h$ 单调不减，对任意有限个两两不交区间 $(c_i,d_i)$，由 $h(d_i)-h(c_i)\ge0$ 得 $g(d_i)-g(c_i)\le V(d_i)-V(c_i)$，故 $\sum_i|g(d_i)-g(c_i)|\le\sum_i(V(d_i)-V(c_i))<\varepsilon$（只要总长 $<\delta$）；$h$ 同理。故 $g,h$ 也绝对连续，最终 $f=g-h$ 绝对连续。两个典型例子说明不等号可以严格：右连续跳跃函数 $\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1]}$ 的跃度被 $V$ 记录但不进入 $f'$；Cantor 函数连续、单调、$C'=0$ a.e.，$V_0^1(C)=1$ 而 $\int|C'|=0$。因此「BV + a.e. 可导」不足以推出绝对连续，等号条件正好筛出 AC 函数。

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$. For a partition $P:a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$, define the variation sum
$$S_P(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|,\qquad
V_a^b(f)=\sup_P S_P(f).$$
If $V_a^b(f)<+\infty$, $f$ is of **bounded variation** on $[a,b]$, written $f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]$. Immediate consequences: using the two-point partition, $V_a^b(f)\ge|f(b)-f(a)|$; $V_a^b(f)=0$ if and only if $f$ is constant; if $f$ is monotone then $V_a^b(f)=|f(b)-f(a)|$ (for an increasing $f$ the variation sum telescopes to $f(b)-f(a)$ and every term is nonnegative). A BV function is bounded:
$$|f(x)|\le|f(a)|+|f(x)-f(a)|\le|f(a)|+V_a^x(f)\le|f(a)|+V_a^b(f).$$
Also remember additivity over intervals: for $a<c<b$,
$$V_a^b(f)=V_a^c(f)+V_c^b(f).$$
Indeed, inserting $c$ into any partition of $[a,b]$ cannot decrease the variation sum, so the supremum may be taken over partitions containing $c$; such a sum splits into the sums over $[a,c]$ and $[c,b]$, and taking suprema gives the identity.

**Jordan decomposition.** If $f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]$, set
$$F(x)=V_a^x(f),\qquad G(x)=F(x)-f(x).$$
By additivity, for $x<y$, $F(y)-F(x)=V_x^y(f)\ge0$, so $F$ is increasing; and
$$G(y)-G(x)=V_x^y(f)-\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)\ge|f(y)-f(x)|-\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)\ge0,$$
so $G$ is increasing too. Hence $f=F-G$ is a difference of two increasing functions. Conversely, if $f=f_1-f_2$ with $f_1,f_2$ increasing, then for any partition,
$$\begin{aligned}
\sum_i|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|
&\le\sum_i|f_1(x_i)-f_1(x_{i-1})|\\
&\quad+\sum_i|f_2(x_i)-f_2(x_{i-1})|\\
&=(f_1(b)-f_1(a))+(f_2(b)-f_2(a))<+\infty,
\end{aligned}$$
so $f\in\mathrm{BV}$. Therefore
$$f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]\iff f=f_1-f_2,\quad f_1,f_2\ \text{increasing}.$$
The decomposition is not unique (adding the same increasing function to both parts preserves it). The symmetric choice
$$f_1=\frac{V_a^x(f)+f(x)}2,\qquad f_2=\frac{V_a^x(f)-f(x)}2$$
consists of increasing functions and has total increase exactly $f_1(b)-f_1(a)+f_2(b)-f_2(a)=V_a^b(f)$.

**Discontinuity structure.** Let $f\in\mathrm{BV}$ and use $f=f_1-f_2$ with $f_1,f_2$ increasing. A monotone function has one-sided limits at every point: $g(x-)=\sup_{t<x}g(t)$ and $g(x+)=\inf_{t>x}g(t)$ (at endpoints only the relevant side), so $f$ has both one-sided limits everywhere. If $g$ is discontinuous at $x$, then $g(x-)<g(x+)$; call this a jump. For $x<y$, $g(x+)\le g(y-)$, so the jump intervals $(g(x-),g(x+))$ are pairwise disjoint. Each nonempty open interval contains a rational, so a monotone function has at most countably many discontinuities. Hence $$D(f)\subseteq D(f_1)\cup D(f_2)$$ is at most countable. A discontinuity may be a jump (the one-sided limits differ) or removable (the one-sided limits agree but the value differs): for example, the function with $f(1/2)=1$ and $f=0$ elsewhere is BV, but has a removable discontinuity at $1/2$. Passing to the right-continuous version $f^+(x)=f(x+)$ (with a suitable definition at the endpoints) changes only countably many points; after that every discontinuity is a jump, and oscillatory discontinuities such as those of $\sin\frac1x$ cannot occur. By contrast, $$g(x)=\sin\frac1x\ (x>0),\qquad g(0)=0$$ is bounded and continuous on $(0,1]$ (except at $0$), but at $x_k=\frac{1}{\pi/2+k\pi}$ it takes the values $(-1)^k$, so the variation sum is at least $2(N-1)$ and $V_0^1(g)=+\infty$: boundedness, even continuity, does not imply bounded variation.

**Almost everywhere differentiability (Lebesgue).** Theorem: every monotone function on $[a,b]$ is differentiable almost everywhere; if $g$ is increasing, then $g'\ge0$ a.e. and
$$\int_a^b g'(t)\,dt\le g(b)-g(a).$$
Sketch: for increasing $g$, consider the four Dini derivatives, e.g.
$$D^+g(x)=\limsup_{h\to0+}\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}h,\qquad
D_-g(x)=\liminf_{h\to0-}\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}h,$$
and the other two; Vitali's covering lemma shows that the sets where two of them differ are null, so all four agree a.e.; their common value is $g'$. The integral inequality follows from Fatou's lemma: extend $g$ constantly beyond $[a,b]$; then
$$\int_a^b\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}h\,dx=\frac1h\Bigl(\int_b^{b+h}g-\int_a^{a+h}g\Bigr)=g(b)-g(a),$$
and letting $h\to0+$ with Fatou gives the claim. For $f\in\mathrm{BV}$, the Jordan decomposition $f=f_1-f_2$ into monotone functions shows that $f'$ exists a.e. The conclusion is almost everywhere, not everywhere: jump points (at most countably many) may be points of non-differentiability.

**Integrability of the derivative and comparison with variation.** By Step 4, $f\in\mathrm{BV}$ is differentiable a.e.; $f'$ is measurable because it is the a.e. limit of the difference quotients $n(f(x+1/n)-f(x))$ (extend $f$ constantly beyond $[a,b]$). Use the symmetric Jordan decomposition
$$f_1=\frac{V_a^x(f)+f(x)}2,\qquad f_2=\frac{V_a^x(f)-f(x)}2,$$
so that $f_1,f_2$ are increasing, $f=f_1-f_2$, and
$$f_1(b)-f_1(a)+f_2(b)-f_2(a)=V_a^b(f).$$
By Step 4, $f_1',f_2'\ge0$ a.e. and $\int_a^b f_i'\le f_i(b)-f_i(a)$. Since $f'=f_1'-f_2'$ a.e., we have $|f'|\le f_1'+f_2'$ a.e., hence
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_a^b|f'(t)|\,dt
&\le\int_a^b f_1'(t)\,dt+\int_a^b f_2'(t)\,dt\\
&\le[f_1(b)-f_1(a)]+[f_2(b)-f_2(a)]=V_a^b(f).
\end{aligned}$$
In particular $f'\in L^1(a,b)$. The inequality can be strict: $g=\mathbf 1_{(1/2,1]}$ on $[0,1]$ has $V_0^1(g)=1$, but $g'=0$ a.e., so $\int_0^1|g'|=0<1$. The jump is recorded by the total variation but is invisible to the derivative.

**Equality characterizes absolute continuity.** For $f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]$, $$V_a^b(f)\ge\int_a^b|f'(t)|\,dt,$$ with equality if and only if $f$ is absolutely continuous. Proof: let $V(x)=V_a^x(f)$ and define $$g(x)=\frac{V(x)+f(x)}2,\qquad h(x)=\frac{V(x)-f(x)}2.$$ For $x<y$, additivity gives $V(y)-V(x)=V_x^y(f)\ge|f(y)-f(x)|$, so both $g$ and $h$ are nondecreasing; also $f=g-h$ and $g+h=V$. Hence $$g(b)-g(a)+h(b)-h(a)=V_a^b(f).$$ Monotone functions are differentiable a.e., so $f'=g'-h'$ a.e. and $g',h'\ge0$. The monotone calculus inequalities $\int_a^b g'\le g(b)-g(a)$ and $\int_a^b h'\le h(b)-h(a)$ give $$\int_a^b|f'|\le\int_a^b(g'+h')\le V_a^b(f).$$ If $f$ is absolutely continuous, then for every partition $\sum_i|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|\le\sum_i\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i}|f'|=\int_a^b|f'|$, so $V_a^b(f)\le\int_a^b|f'|$; combined with the reverse inequality, equality holds. Conversely, if equality holds, set $H(x)=V(x)-\int_a^x|f'|$. For $x<y$, applying the inequality above on $[x,y]$ gives $H(y)\ge H(x)$; also $H\ge0$ and $H(b)=0$, so $H\equiv0$. Thus $V(x)=\int_a^x|f'|$ is absolutely continuous. Since $g+h=V$ with $g,h$ nondecreasing, for any finite family of pairwise disjoint intervals $(c_i,d_i)$, $h(d_i)-h(c_i)\ge0$ gives $g(d_i)-g(c_i)\le V(d_i)-V(c_i)$, hence $\sum_i|g(d_i)-g(c_i)|\le\sum_i(V(d_i)-V(c_i))<\varepsilon$ whenever the total length is $<\delta$; the same holds for $h$. Thus $g,h$ are absolutely continuous and $f=g-h$ is absolutely continuous. Two examples show strict inequality: the right-continuous jump function $\mathbf 1_{[1/2,1]}$ has its jump recorded by $V$ but not by $f'$; the Cantor function is continuous and increasing with $C'=0$ a.e., $V_0^1(C)=1$ while $\int|C'|=0$. Thus 'BV plus a.e. differentiability' does not imply absolute continuity; the equality case singles out exactly the AC functions.

设 $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$。若对任意 $\varepsilon>0$，存在 $\delta>0$，使得对 $[a,b]$ 中任意**有限个两两不交**的开区间 $(a_i,b_i)$，只要
$$\sum_i(b_i-a_i)<\delta,$$
就有
$$\sum_i|f(b_i)-f(a_i)|<\varepsilon,$$
则称 $f$ 在 $[a,b]$ 上**绝对连续**，记 $f\in AC[a,b]$。要点有三：$\delta$ 只依赖 $\varepsilon$，不依赖区间的个数与位置；区间必须两两不交；控制的是**总和**，不是单个区间。若只要求单个区间，就是一致连续；所以
$$AC\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{一致连续},$$
反之不成立（Cantor 函数连续、从而一致连续，却不 AC，见第 6 步）。定义中的有限族可以换成可数族：对可数不交区间取前 $N$ 项，部分和 $<\varepsilon$，令 $N\to\infty$ 得可数和不大于 $\varepsilon$；由于 $\varepsilon$ 任意，这与原定义等价。

**AC ⇒ BV**。取 $\varepsilon=1$，得 $\delta>0$：任意有限个不交区间总长 $<\delta$ 时，增量的绝对值之和 $<1$。设 $P:a=x_0<\cdots<x_n=b$ 是任意分割。称长度 $\ge\delta$ 的小区间为长区间，其个数 $N\le(b-a)/\delta$。每个长区间的贡献 $\le2M$，其中 $M=\sup_{[a,b]}|f|<+\infty$（AC ⇒ 连续 ⇒ 有界）。剩下的小区间长度 $<\delta$；把相邻的短区间合并成块，使每块总长 $<\delta$，并在将下一段并入就会达到 $\delta$ 时另起一块。每块由 AC（$\varepsilon=1$）贡献 $<1$。在每一段连续的短区间中，相邻两块的总长至少为 $\delta$（否则前一块本可再并入下一块的第一段），故该段的块数不超过 $2(b-a)/\delta+1$；长区间至多把短区间分成 $N+1$ 段。于是对任意分割，
$$S_P(f)\le2MN+(N+1)\Bigl(\frac{2(b-a)}{\delta}+1\Bigr),$$
右边与 $P$ 无关且有限，故 $V_a^b(f)<+\infty$，即 $f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]$。

**包含关系与反例**。综合上面的结果：
$$\begin{aligned}
&\text{Lipschitz}\ \Longrightarrow\ AC\\
&\quad\Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{BV}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{a.e. 可导}.
\end{aligned}$$
Lipschitz ⇒ AC：若 $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|$，取 $\delta=\varepsilon/L$ 即可。AC ⇒ BV 是第 2 步；BV ⇒ a.e. 可导是 Lebesgue 定理。反向全部不成立：
- $f(x)=\sqrt x$ 在 $[0,1]$ 上 AC。直接验证：对不交区间，
$$\sum_i(\sqrt{b_i}-\sqrt{a_i})\le\sqrt{\sum_i(b_i-a_i)},$$
故取 $\delta=\varepsilon^2$ 即可（也可由 $f'=\frac1{2\sqrt x}\in L^1(0,1)$ 与第 5 步的 FTC 判定）。但 $\frac{|f(h)-f(0)|}{h}=\frac1{\sqrt h}\to\infty$，故不是 Lipschitz。
- Cantor 函数连续、单调、有界变差，但不 AC（第 6 步）。
- $f(x)=x^2\sin\frac1{x^2}$（$f(0)=0$）在 $[0,1]$ 上处处可导；当 $x>0$ 时
$$f'(x)=2x\sin\frac1{x^2}-\frac2x\cos\frac1{x^2},$$
且 $\int_0^1|f'|=+\infty$（第二项经 $u=1/x^2$ 化为 $\int_1^\infty\frac{|\cos u|}{u}du=+\infty$）；由有界变差一节的不等式（若 $f\in\mathrm{BV}$ 则 $\int|f'|\le V$）得 $V_0^1(f)=+\infty$。所以「a.e. 可导」也不蕴涵 BV。
- $f(x)=|x|$ 在 $[-1,1]$ 上 Lipschitz 从而 AC，但在 $0$ 不可导；所以 AC 不蕴涵处处可导，只蕴涵 a.e. 可导。
- Cantor 函数还是一致连续的，所以「一致连续 ⇒ AC」也不成立。

记住：链条只能从左往右推；每个反例都只否定一个反向箭头。

**不定积分是 AC**。设 $g\in L^1(a,b)$，$F(x)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt$。先证 $F$ 绝对连续。用积分的绝对连续性：对 $\varepsilon>0$，取 $M>0$ 足够大，令 $g_M=g\mathbf 1_{\{|g|\le M\}}$，使 $\|g-g_M\|_1<\varepsilon/2$（由控制收敛定理），再取 $\delta=\varepsilon/(2M)$。若可测集 $E$ 满足 $m(E)<\delta$，则
$$\int_E|g|\le\int_E|g_M|+\frac\varepsilon2\le M m(E)+\frac\varepsilon2<\varepsilon.$$
对有限个不交区间 $(a_i,b_i)$，令 $E=\bigcup_i(a_i,b_i)$；若 $\sum(b_i-a_i)<\delta$，则 $m(E)<\delta$，于是
$$\sum_i|F(b_i)-F(a_i)|\le\sum_i\int_{a_i}^{b_i}|g|=\int_E|g|<\varepsilon.$$
故 $F\in AC[a,b]$。再由勒贝格微分定理（下一节），$F'=g$ a.e.。因此每个 $L^1$ 函数的变上限积分都是 AC 函数，并且是 $g$ 的一个原函数（a.e. 意义下）。反过来，若 $f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^x h(t)\,dt$ 对某个 $h\in L^1$ 成立，则 $f$ 是 AC 函数加常数，故 $f\in AC$，且 $f'=h$ a.e.。

**AC 版本的微积分基本定理**。设 $f\in AC[a,b]$。由第 2 步 $f\in\mathrm{BV}$，由 BV 的 Lebesgue 定理，$f'$ 存在 a.e. 且 $f'\in L^1(a,b)$。令
$$F(x)=\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt.$$
由第 4 步，$F\in AC[a,b]$ 且 $F'=f'$ a.e.。于是 $g=f-F$ 绝对连续，且 $g'=0$ a.e.。**引理**：若 $g\in AC[a,b]$ 且 $g'=0$ a.e.，则 $g$ 为常数。证明要点：对任意 $[c,d]\subseteq[a,b]$ 和 $\varepsilon>0$，取 AC 定义中的 $\delta$；零测集 $\{g'\ne0\}$ 可被总长 $<\delta$ 的开区间覆盖；在其余点，$g$ 的差商任意小；用 Vitali 覆盖引理取出有限个互不相交的区间覆盖 $[c,d]$（除总长可任意小的一段），好区间上的增量 $<\varepsilon$ 倍长度，坏区间连同剩余小段的总增量由 AC 控制 $<2\varepsilon$，故 $|g(d)-g(c)|\le\varepsilon(d-c)+2\varepsilon$；令 $\varepsilon\to0$ 得 $g(c)=g(d)$。于是 $g$ 为常数；由 $g(a)=f(a)-F(a)=f(a)$ 得
$$f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt\qquad(\forall x\in[a,b]).$$
结合第 4 步，得到充要条件：
$$\begin{aligned}
f\in AC[a,b]\iff{}&f'\ \text{存在 a.e.},\ f'\in L^1(a,b),\\
&\text{且}\ f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt\ (\forall x).
\end{aligned}$$
条件缺一不可：仅有「a.e. 可导 + 导数可积」不够，Cantor 函数就是反例（第 6 步）。

**Cantor 函数（魔鬼阶梯）**。在 $[0,1]$ 上递归挖去中间三分之一：第一步挖去 $(1/3,2/3)$，第二步在剩下的两个区间中各挖去中间三分之一，如此继续；在每次挖去的开区间上令 $C$ 为常数，并用连续性延拓，得到连续、单调增的 $C$，满足 $C(0)=0$、$C(1)=1$。挖去的开区间总长度为
$$\frac13+\frac29+\frac4{27}+\cdots=\frac{1/3}{1-2/3}=1,$$
故 Cantor 集 $K$ 的勒贝格测度为 $0$。$C$ 在每个挖去的区间上为常数，所以 $C'=0$ 在 $K^c$ 上处处成立；$m(K)=0$，故
$$C'=0\quad\text{a.e.},\qquad \int_0^1|C'(t)|\,dt=0.$$
但 $C$ 单调增，$V_0^1(C)=C(1)-C(0)=1$。如果 $C$ 绝对连续，第 5 步的 FTC 将给出
$$1=C(1)-C(0)=\int_0^1 C'(t)\,dt=0,$$
矛盾！所以 $C\notin AC[0,1]$。它连续、单调、有界变差、a.e. 可导，甚至 $C'\in L^1$，却仍不绝对连续；这说明「a.e. 可导 + 导数可积」远不足以保证 FTC，公式 $f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x f'$ 才是 AC 的本质。注意：$C$ 不是「AC 版本 FTC」的反例（该定理假设 AC），而是「去掉 AC 后 FTC 仍成立」的反例；它把零测的 Cantor 集映满 $[0,1]$，故也不具有 AC 函数必有的 Luzin $N$ 性质（零测集映为零测集）。
en:
Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$. We say $f$ is **absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$, written $f\in AC[a,b]$, if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that for every finite family of pairwise disjoint open intervals $(a_i,b_i)\subset[a,b]$,
$$\sum_i(b_i-a_i)<\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_i|f(b_i)-f(a_i)|<\varepsilon.$$
Three points are essential: $\delta$ depends only on $\varepsilon$, not on the number or location of the intervals; the intervals must be pairwise disjoint; and the estimate controls the whole sum, not a single interval. If only one interval were required, this would be uniform continuity; hence
$$AC\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{uniformly continuous},$$
but not conversely (the Cantor function is continuous, hence uniformly continuous, but not AC; see Step 6). Finite families may be replaced by countable families: for countably many disjoint intervals, apply the estimate to the first $N$ and let $N\to\infty$; the countable sum is at most $\varepsilon$, and since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary this is equivalent to the original definition.

**AC implies BV.** Take $\varepsilon=1$ and let $\delta>0$ be the corresponding modulus: for any finite disjoint family with total length $<\delta$, the sum of the absolute increments is $<1$. Let $P:a=x_0<\cdots<x_n=b$ be any partition. Call an interval long if its length is $\ge\delta$; there are at most $N\le(b-a)/\delta$ of them, and each contributes at most $2M$, where $M=\sup_{[a,b]}|f|<+\infty$ (AC implies continuity, hence boundedness). The remaining intervals are short (length $<\delta$); group consecutive short intervals into blocks of total length $<\delta$, starting a new block when adding the next interval would reach $\delta$. Each block contributes $<1$ by AC with $\varepsilon=1$. Within each run of consecutive short intervals, two consecutive blocks have total length at least $\delta$ (otherwise the first could have absorbed the first interval of the second), so the run contains at most $2(b-a)/\delta+1$ blocks; the long intervals split the short intervals into at most $N+1$ runs. Therefore, for every partition,
$$S_P(f)\le2MN+(N+1)\Bigl(\frac{2(b-a)}{\delta}+1\Bigr),$$
a bound independent of $P$ and finite. Hence $V_a^b(f)<+\infty$, i.e. $f\in\mathrm{BV}[a,b]$.

**Inclusions and counterexamples.** Combining the results,
$$\begin{aligned}
&\text{Lipschitz}\ \Longrightarrow\ AC\\
&\quad\Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{BV}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{differentiable a.e.}
\end{aligned}$$
Lipschitz implies AC: if $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|$, take $\delta=\varepsilon/L$. AC implies BV by Step 2, and BV implies a.e. differentiability by Lebesgue's theorem. None of the arrows reverses:
- $f(x)=\sqrt x$ is AC on $[0,1]$. Directly, for disjoint intervals,
$$\sum_i(\sqrt{b_i}-\sqrt{a_i})\le\sqrt{\sum_i(b_i-a_i)},$$
so $\delta=\varepsilon^2$ works (equivalently, $f'=1/(2\sqrt x)\in L^1(0,1)$ and the FTC of Step 5 applies). But $|f(h)-f(0)|/h=1/\sqrt h\to\infty$, so it is not Lipschitz.
- The Cantor function is continuous, increasing and BV, but not AC (Step 6).
- $f(x)=x^2\sin\frac1{x^2}$ (with $f(0)=0$) is differentiable everywhere on $[0,1]$; for $x>0$,
$$f'(x)=2x\sin\frac1{x^2}-\frac2x\cos\frac1{x^2},$$
and $\int_0^1|f'|=+\infty$ (the second term becomes $\int_1^\infty\frac{|\cos u|}{u}du=+\infty$ under $u=1/x^2$); by the inequality from the BV section (if $f\in\mathrm{BV}$ then $\int|f'|\le V$), $V_0^1(f)=+\infty$. Thus 'a.e. differentiable' does not imply BV either.
- $f(x)=|x|$ on $[-1,1]$ is Lipschitz, hence AC, but is not differentiable at $0$; so AC does not imply differentiability everywhere, only a.e.
- The Cantor function is also uniformly continuous, so 'uniformly continuous implies AC' is false.

Remember: the chain only goes from left to right; each counterexample refutes only one reverse arrow.

**Indefinite integrals are AC.** Let $g\in L^1(a,b)$ and $F(x)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt$. First prove that $F$ is absolutely continuous. Use absolute continuity of the Lebesgue integral: for $\varepsilon>0$, choose $M>0$ large enough and set $g_M=g\mathbf 1_{\{|g|\le M\}}$ so that $\|g-g_M\|_1<\varepsilon/2$ (by dominated convergence), then take $\delta=\varepsilon/(2M)$. If a measurable set $E$ has $m(E)<\delta$, then
$$\int_E|g|\le\int_E|g_M|+\frac\varepsilon2\le M m(E)+\frac\varepsilon2<\varepsilon.$$
For finitely many disjoint intervals $(a_i,b_i)$, let $E=\bigcup_i(a_i,b_i)$; if $\sum(b_i-a_i)<\delta$, then $m(E)<\delta$, so
$$\sum_i|F(b_i)-F(a_i)|\le\sum_i\int_{a_i}^{b_i}|g|=\int_E|g|<\varepsilon.$$
Hence $F\in AC[a,b]$. By the Lebesgue differentiation theorem (next section), $F'=g$ a.e. Thus every indefinite integral of an $L^1$ function is AC and is an antiderivative of $g$ in the a.e. sense. Conversely, if $f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^x h(t)\,dt$ for some $h\in L^1$, then $f$ is AC plus a constant, so $f\in AC$ and $f'=h$ a.e.

**The AC version of the fundamental theorem of calculus.** Let $f\in AC[a,b]$. By Step 2, $f\in\mathrm{BV}$; by the BV differentiability theorem, $f'$ exists a.e. and $f'\in L^1(a,b)$. Set
$$F(x)=\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt.$$
By Step 4, $F\in AC[a,b]$ and $F'=f'$ a.e. Hence $g=f-F$ is absolutely continuous and $g'=0$ a.e. **Lemma**: if $g\in AC[a,b]$ and $g'=0$ a.e., then $g$ is constant. Sketch: for any $[c,d]\subseteq[a,b]$ and $\varepsilon>0$, take $\delta$ from the AC definition; the null set $\{g'\ne0\}$ can be covered by open intervals of total length $<\delta$; at every other point the difference quotients of $g$ are arbitrarily small; Vitali's covering lemma extracts finitely many pairwise disjoint intervals covering $[c,d]$ except a set of arbitrarily small length; the good intervals contribute $<\varepsilon$ times their length, while the bad intervals together with the remaining small set contribute $<2\varepsilon$ by AC; hence $|g(d)-g(c)|\le\varepsilon(d-c)+2\varepsilon$; letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $g(c)=g(d)$. Thus $g$ is constant, and $g(a)=f(a)-F(a)=f(a)$ yields
$$f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt\qquad(\forall x\in[a,b]).$$
Together with Step 4 this gives the characterization
$$\begin{aligned}
f\in AC[a,b]\iff{}&f'\ \text{exists a.e.},\ f'\in L^1(a,b),\\
&\text{and}\ f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt\ (\forall x).
\end{aligned}$$
No condition is redundant: 'a.e. differentiable with integrable derivative' alone is not enough, as the Cantor function shows (Step 6).

**The Cantor function (devil's staircase).** Recursively remove the middle third from $[0,1]$: first $(1/3,2/3)$, then the middle third of each remaining interval, and so on; on each removed open interval let $C$ be constant, and extend continuously. This gives a continuous, increasing $C$ with $C(0)=0$ and $C(1)=1$. The removed intervals have total length
$$\frac13+\frac29+\frac4{27}+\cdots=\frac{1/3}{1-2/3}=1,$$
so the Cantor set $K$ has Lebesgue measure $0$. Since $C$ is constant on every removed interval, $C'=0$ everywhere on $K^c$; as $m(K)=0$,
$$C'=0\quad\text{a.e.},\qquad \int_0^1|C'(t)|\,dt=0.$$
But $C$ is increasing, so $V_0^1(C)=C(1)-C(0)=1$. If $C$ were absolutely continuous, the FTC of Step 5 would give
$$1=C(1)-C(0)=\int_0^1 C'(t)\,dt=0,$$
a contradiction. Hence $C\notin AC[0,1]$. It is continuous, increasing, BV, differentiable a.e., and even $C'\in L^1$, yet not absolutely continuous; this shows that 'a.e. differentiable with integrable derivative' is far from sufficient for the FTC, and that the formula $f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x f'$ is the essence of AC. Note: $C$ is not a counterexample to the AC version of the FTC (which assumes AC); it is a counterexample to the claim that the FTC remains true after AC is dropped. It maps the null Cantor set onto $[0,1]$, so it also fails Luzin's $N$ property (null sets map to null sets), which every AC function has.

zh: 设 $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$（在每个紧集上可积）。对 $x\in\mathbb R$、$r>0$，定义滑动平均 $$A_rf(x)=\frac1{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}f(t)\,dt.$$ **勒贝格微分定理**：$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)\qquad\text{对 a.e. }x\in\mathbb R.$$ 更强的逐点概念：称 $x$ 为 $f$ 的**勒贝格点**，若 $$\lim_{r\to0^+}\frac1{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(t)-f(x)|\,dt=0.$$ 定理可加强为「几乎处处的点都是勒贝格点」：勒贝格点显然给出 $|A_rf(x)-f(x)|\le A_r|f-f(x)|(x)\to0$；反过来需要第 5 步的论证，平均收敛本身并不自动给出绝对值的平均收敛。条件只要求局部可积，不要求连续或有界。结论是 a.e.，不能加强为处处：$f=\mathbf 1_{(0,\infty)}$ 在 $x=0$ 处 $A_rf(0)=\frac12\to\frac12\ne f(0)=0$，而 $\{0\}$ 是零测集。改变零测集上的值不改变任何积分平均，所以定理本质上只能是 a.e. 的；但个别坏点可以通过改值匹配平均极限，不能改进的是「对所有函数处处成立」这一整体结论。

**连续情形**。若 $f$ 在 $x$ 连续，则
$$\begin{aligned}
|A_rf(x)-f(x)|
&\le\frac1{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(t)-f(x)|\,dt\\
&\le\sup_{|t-x|\le r}|f(t)-f(x)|\to0\qquad(r\to0^+).
\end{aligned}$$
故每个连续点都是勒贝格点；特别地，连续函数的滑动平均在每一点收敛。若 $f$ 在紧集上一致连续，则收敛在该紧集上一致。但这对一般 $L^1$ 函数不够：可测函数可以处处不连续却仍属于 $L^1$（如 $\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}=0$ a.e.），所以必须用「连续函数在 $L^1$ 中稠密」把结论转移到一般 $f$。第 3、4 步就是完成这个转移。

**极大函数与弱 $(1,1)$ 估计**。对 $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ 定义
$$Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac1{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(t)|\,dt.$$
则对每个 $\lambda>0$，
$$\bigl|\{x:Mf(x)>\lambda\}\bigr|\le\frac3\lambda\|f\|_1.$$
证明：设 $E_\lambda=\{Mf>\lambda\}$。对每个 $x\in E_\lambda$，取以 $x$ 为中心、半径 $r_x$ 的区间 $I_x$，使 $\frac1{|I_x|}\int_{I_x}|f|>\lambda$。由 Vitali 覆盖引理，从 $\{I_x\}$ 中取出可数个两两不交的区间 $I_1,I_2,\dots$，使 $E_\lambda\subseteq\bigcup_j3I_j$。于是
$$\begin{aligned}
|E_\lambda|
&\le\sum_j|3I_j|=3\sum_j|I_j|\\
&<\frac3\lambda\sum_j\int_{I_j}|f|
\le\frac3\lambda\|f\|_1.
\end{aligned}$$
常数 $3$ 不是最优的；关键是它与 $f$ 无关。由估计还可得 $Mf<+\infty$ a.e.：对每个 $N$，$\{Mf>N\}$ 的测度 $\le3\|f\|_1/N$，令 $N\to\infty$ 即得 $\{Mf=+\infty\}$ 为零测集。

**稠密逼近：一般 $f\in L^1$**。取连续、紧支集的 $g$ 使 $\|f-g\|_1<\varepsilon$（连续紧支函数在 $L^1$ 中稠密），令 $h=f-g$。对每个 $x$，
$$|A_rf(x)-A_rg(x)|\le A_r|h|(x)\le Mh(x).$$
由第 2 步，$A_rg(x)\to g(x)$ 对每个 $x$ 成立。于是
$$\limsup_{r\to0}A_rf(x)\le g(x)+Mh(x),\qquad
\liminf_{r\to0}A_rf(x)\ge g(x)-Mh(x),$$
故振幅 $O(x)=\limsup_{r\to0}A_rf(x)-\liminf_{r\to0}A_rf(x)$ 满足 $O(x)\le2Mh(x)$。对 $\lambda>0$，
$$\begin{aligned}
\{O>2\lambda\}&\subseteq\{Mh>\lambda\},\\
|\{O>2\lambda\}|&\le\frac3\lambda\|h\|_1<\frac{3\varepsilon}{\lambda}.
\end{aligned}$$
令 $\varepsilon\to0$，得 $|\{O>2\lambda\}|=0$；再对 $\lambda=1/n$ 取并，得 $O=0$ a.e.。所以 $A_rf$ 在 a.e. 点收敛到某个 $L(x)$。最后识别 $L=f$：由 $\|A_rf\|_1\le\|f\|_1$（滑动平均是 $L^1$ 压缩），
$$\begin{aligned}
\|A_rf-f\|_1
&\le\|A_r(f-g)\|_1+\|A_rg-g\|_1+\|g-f\|_1\\
&\le2\varepsilon+\|A_rg-g\|_1.
\end{aligned}$$
$g$ 连续紧支，$A_rg\to g$ 在支集上一致且由控制收敛 $\|A_rg-g\|_1\to0$。故 $A_rf\to f$ 于 $L^1$。a.e. 收敛的极限 $L$ 与 $L^1$ 极限 $f$ 必 a.e. 相等（若序列在 $L^1$ 中收敛到 $f$，其子列 a.e. 收敛到 $f$；而 a.e. 极限唯一），所以 $L=f$ a.e.。这就证明了 $A_rf\to f$ a.e.。$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ 的情形用紧区间截断（区间外取 $0$）即可。

**勒贝格点**。先设 $f\in L^1$（局部情形在紧区间上截断）。对每个有理数 $q$，函数 $|f-q|\in L^1$，由第 4 步，存在零测集 $N_q$，使 $x\notin N_q$ 时
$$A_r|f-q|(x)\to|f(x)-q|.$$
令 $N=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}N_q$，则 $N$ 零测（可数并）。取 $x\notin N$ 且 $|f(x)|<+\infty$（后者对 a.e. $x$ 成立，因为 $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$）。对任意 $\varepsilon>0$，取 $q\in\mathbb Q$ 使 $|f(x)-q|<\varepsilon$。则
$$\begin{aligned}
A_r|f-f(x)|(x)
&\le A_r|f-q|(x)+|q-f(x)|\\
&\to|f(x)-q|+|q-f(x)|<2\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}$$
所以 $\limsup_{r\to0}A_r|f-f(x)|(x)\le2\varepsilon$ 对一切 $\varepsilon>0$，故极限为 $0$：$x$ 是勒贝格点。于是 a.e. 点是勒贝格点；反之，勒贝格点满足
$$|A_rf(x)-f(x)|\le A_r|f-f(x)|(x)\to0,$$
故第 1 步的定理成立。把 $f=\mathbf 1_E$（$E$ 可测）代入，得到**勒贝格密度定理**：
$$\lim_{r\to0}\frac{m(E\cap(x-r,x+r))}{2r}=\mathbf 1_E(x)\qquad(\text{a.e. }x).$$
即几乎每个点要么是 $E$ 的密度点（密度 $1$），要么是 $E^c$ 的密度点（密度 $0$）。局部情形对每个紧区间重复上述论证（可数并仍为零测），结论不变。

**推论与应用**。(i) 不定积分：若 $g\in L^1(a,b)$，$F(x)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt$，则对 a.e. $x\in(a,b)$，
$$F'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}g(t)\,dt=g(x).$$
这里用的是对以 $x$ 为端点、长度趋于 $0$ 的区间也成立的版本；证明与中心区间平行（把极大函数中的中心区间换成含 $x$ 的区间，弱估计的常数可能改变，但不影响结论）。故由第 4 步得 $F'=g$ a.e.。于是 $F\in AC[a,b]$，这正是 AC 版本 FTC 的一半。(ii) 单调函数：若 $f$ 单调增，先取右连续正规化 $\tilde f(x)=f(x+)$；它只改至多可数多个点，故 a.e. 导数不变。对 $\tilde f$ 构造 Lebesgue–Stieltjes 测度 $\mu_{\tilde f}((c,d])=\tilde f(d)-\tilde f(c)$；对 $\mu_{\tilde f}$ 的 Lebesgue 分解用密度定理，得 $f'=\frac{d\mu_{\tilde f}^{ac}}{dx}$ a.e.，故单调函数 a.e. 可导，且
$$\int_a^b f'(t)\,dt\le f(b)-f(a).$$
由 Jordan 分解，$f\in\mathrm{BV}$ 也 a.e. 可导，且 $\int_a^b|f'|\le V_a^b(f)$。(iii) 结论是 a.e.：跳跃函数的平均在跳跃点收敛到左右极限的中点（如 $\mathbf 1_{(0,\infty)}$ 在 $0$ 处为 $1/2$），所以坏点集可以非空；但它是零测集。勒贝格微分定理不声称 $f$ 连续，也不声称平均在每点收敛。
en: Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ (integrable on every compact set). For $x\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$, define the sliding average $$A_rf(x)=\frac1{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}f(t)\,dt.$$ The **Lebesgue differentiation theorem** states $$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\mathbb R.$$ A stronger pointwise notion: $x$ is a **Lebesgue point** of $f$ if $$\lim_{r\to0^+}\frac1{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(t)-f(x)|\,dt=0.$$ The theorem can be strengthened to 'almost every point is a Lebesgue point': a Lebesgue point plainly gives $|A_rf(x)-f(x)|\le A_r|f-f(x)|(x)\to0$; the converse needs the argument of Step 5, since convergence of the average alone does not automatically give convergence of the average of the absolute deviation. The hypothesis is local integrability only; no continuity or boundedness is assumed. The conclusion is a.e. and cannot be strengthened to everywhere: for $f=\mathbf 1_{(0,\infty)}$ at $x=0$, $A_rf(0)=\frac12\to\frac12\ne f(0)=0$, and $\{0\}$ is null. Values on null sets do not affect any integral average, so the theorem is intrinsically a.e.; individual bad points can still be matched by changing their values, but the statement cannot hold everywhere for all functions.

**The continuous case.** If $f$ is continuous at $x$, then
$$\begin{aligned}
|A_rf(x)-f(x)|
&\le\frac1{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(t)-f(x)|\,dt\\
&\le\sup_{|t-x|\le r}|f(t)-f(x)|\to0\qquad(r\to0^+).
\end{aligned}$$
Thus every continuity point is a Lebesgue point; in particular, for a continuous function the sliding averages converge at every point. If $f$ is uniformly continuous on a compact set, the convergence is uniform there. This is not enough for a general $L^1$ function: a measurable function can be everywhere discontinuous and still belong to $L^1$ (e.g. $\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}=0$ a.e.). One must transfer the conclusion to general $f$ using the density of continuous functions in $L^1$; Steps 3 and 4 carry this out.

**The maximal function and the weak $(1,1)$ estimate.** For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ define
$$Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac1{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(t)|\,dt.$$
Then for every $\lambda>0$,
$$\bigl|\{x:Mf(x)>\lambda\}\bigr|\le\frac3\lambda\|f\|_1.$$
Proof: let $E_\lambda=\{Mf>\lambda\}$. For each $x\in E_\lambda$ choose an interval $I_x$ centered at $x$, of radius $r_x$, such that $\frac1{|I_x|}\int_{I_x}|f|>\lambda$. By Vitali's covering lemma, select countably many pairwise disjoint intervals $I_1,I_2,\dots$ from $\{I_x\}$ with $E_\lambda\subseteq\bigcup_j3I_j$. Then
$$\begin{aligned}
|E_\lambda|
&\le\sum_j|3I_j|=3\sum_j|I_j|\\
&<\frac3\lambda\sum_j\int_{I_j}|f|
\le\frac3\lambda\|f\|_1.
\end{aligned}$$
The constant $3$ is not optimal; what matters is that it is independent of $f$. The estimate also gives $Mf<+\infty$ a.e.: for every $N$, $|\{Mf>N\}|\le3\|f\|_1/N$, so letting $N\to\infty$ shows that $\{Mf=+\infty\}$ is null.

**Density approximation: general $f\in L^1$.** Choose continuous compactly supported $g$ with $\|f-g\|_1<\varepsilon$ (continuous compactly supported functions are dense in $L^1$), and put $h=f-g$. For every $x$,
$$|A_rf(x)-A_rg(x)|\le A_r|h|(x)\le Mh(x).$$
By Step 2, $A_rg(x)\to g(x)$ for every $x$. Hence
$$\limsup_{r\to0}A_rf(x)\le g(x)+Mh(x),\qquad
\liminf_{r\to0}A_rf(x)\ge g(x)-Mh(x),$$
so the oscillation $O(x)=\limsup_{r\to0}A_rf(x)-\liminf_{r\to0}A_rf(x)$ satisfies $O(x)\le2Mh(x)$. For $\lambda>0$,
$$\begin{aligned}
\{O>2\lambda\}&\subseteq\{Mh>\lambda\},\\
|\{O>2\lambda\}|&\le\frac3\lambda\|h\|_1<\frac{3\varepsilon}{\lambda}.
\end{aligned}$$
Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $|\{O>2\lambda\}|=0$; taking the union over $\lambda=1/n$ gives $O=0$ a.e. Thus $A_rf$ converges a.e. to some $L(x)$. Finally identify $L=f$: since $\|A_rf\|_1\le\|f\|_1$ (the sliding average is an $L^1$ contraction),
$$\begin{aligned}
\|A_rf-f\|_1
&\le\|A_r(f-g)\|_1+\|A_rg-g\|_1+\|g-f\|_1\\
&\le2\varepsilon+\|A_rg-g\|_1.
\end{aligned}$$
For continuous compactly supported $g$, $A_rg\to g$ uniformly on the support and $\|A_rg-g\|_1\to0$ by dominated convergence. Hence $A_rf\to f$ in $L^1$. An a.e. limit $L$ and an $L^1$ limit $f$ must agree a.e. (an $L^1$ convergent sequence has a subsequence converging a.e. to its limit, and a.e. limits are unique), so $L=f$ a.e. This proves $A_rf\to f$ a.e. The $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ case follows by truncating to compact intervals (setting $f=0$ outside).

**Lebesgue points.** First assume $f\in L^1$ (the local case follows by truncating to compact intervals). For every rational $q$, the function $|f-q|$ belongs to $L^1$, so by Step 4 there is a null set $N_q$ such that for $x\notin N_q$,
$$A_r|f-q|(x)\to|f(x)-q|.$$
Let $N=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}N_q$; it is null (a countable union). Take $x\notin N$ with $|f(x)|<+\infty$ (the latter holds for a.e. $x$, since $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$). For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $q\in\mathbb Q$ with $|f(x)-q|<\varepsilon$. Then
$$\begin{aligned}
A_r|f-f(x)|(x)
&\le A_r|f-q|(x)+|q-f(x)|\\
&\to|f(x)-q|+|q-f(x)|<2\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $\limsup_{r\to0}A_r|f-f(x)|(x)\le2\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so the limit is $0$: $x$ is a Lebesgue point. Thus a.e. point is a Lebesgue point; conversely, a Lebesgue point satisfies
$$|A_rf(x)-f(x)|\le A_r|f-f(x)|(x)\to0,$$
so the theorem of Step 1 holds. Taking $f=\mathbf 1_E$ for a measurable $E$ gives the **Lebesgue density theorem**:
$$\lim_{r\to0}\frac{m(E\cap(x-r,x+r))}{2r}=\mathbf 1_E(x)\qquad(\text{a.e. }x).$$
That is, at almost every point either $E$ has density $1$ or $E^c$ has density $1$. For the local case, repeat the argument on each compact interval; the union of countably many null sets is still null.

**Corollaries and applications.** (i) Indefinite integrals: if $g\in L^1(a,b)$ and $F(x)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt$, then for a.e. $x\in(a,b)$,
$$F'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}g(t)\,dt=g(x).$$
Here one uses the version for intervals with endpoint $x$ and length tending to $0$; its proof parallels the centered case (replace centered intervals in the maximal function by intervals containing $x$; the constant in the weak estimate may change, which does not affect the conclusion). Hence Step 4 gives $F'=g$ a.e. Therefore $F\in AC[a,b]$, which is one half of the AC version of the FTC. (ii) Monotone functions: if $f$ is increasing, first take the right-continuous regularization $\tilde f(x)=f(x+)$; it changes only countably many points and hence not the a.e. derivative. For $\tilde f$ construct the Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure $\mu_{\tilde f}((c,d])=\tilde f(d)-\tilde f(c)$; applying the density theorem to the Lebesgue decomposition of $\mu_{\tilde f}$ gives $f'=\frac{d\mu_{\tilde f}^{ac}}{dx}$ a.e., so every monotone function is differentiable a.e. and
$$\int_a^b f'(t)\,dt\le f(b)-f(a).$$
By Jordan decomposition, every $f\in\mathrm{BV}$ is differentiable a.e. and $\int_a^b|f'|\le V_a^b(f)$. (iii) The conclusion is a.e.: the averages of a jump function at the jump converge to the midpoint of the one-sided limits (e.g. $\mathbf 1_{(0,\infty)}$ gives $1/2$ at $0$), so the bad set can be nonempty; it is nevertheless null. The Lebesgue differentiation theorem does not claim that $f$ is continuous, nor that the averages converge at every point.
